body: == (loose equality) converts types before comparing: '5' == 5 is true. === (strict equality) checks both value AND type: '5' === 5 is false. Always use === in professional code to avoid unexpected bugs. The only useful exception is == null which checks for both null and undefined.

The event loop is the mechanism that allows Node.js/JavaScript to perform non-blocking operations. It continuously checks the call stack and callback queue. Order: Call Stack → Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) → Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O). When the call stack is empty, it picks the next task from the microtask queue first, then macrotask queue.

Object.freeze() makes an object completely immutable — you cannot add, remove, or modify properties. Object.seal() allows modification of existing properties but prevents adding or removing properties.

const frozen = Object.freeze({ a: 1, b: 2 });
frozen.a = 10; // Silently fails (strict mode throws)
frozen.c = 3; // Silently fails

const sealed = Object.seal({ a: 1, b: 2 });
sealed.a = 10; // Works! (modification allowed)
sealed.c = 3; // Fails (no new properties)
delete sealed.a; // Fails (no deletion)

Both are shallow — nested objects are NOT affected.

const prevents reassignment of the variable binding, but the object itself is still mutable. Object.freeze() makes the object's properties immutable.

const obj = { name: 'Siva' };
obj.name = 'Chitti'; // Works! const doesn't freeze properties
obj = {}; // Error! const prevents reassignment

const frozen = Object.freeze({ name: 'Siva' });
frozen.name = 'Chitti'; // Fails! Properties are frozen

Use const + Object.freeze() together for truly immutable objects.

Object.prototype is the top of the prototype chain for all JavaScript objects. Every object inherits methods like toString(), hasOwnProperty(), valueOf() from Object.prototype. When you access a property on an object, JS first looks on the object itself, then walks up the prototype chain until it reaches Object.prototype (then null).

const obj = { name: 'Siva' };
obj.toString(); // Inherited from Object.prototype
obj.hasOwnProperty('name'); // true — also inherited

Object.prototype is essentially the 'grandfather' of all objects.

Lazy loading improves initial page load time by loading modules/components only when needed (e.g., when a user navigates to a route). Impact: (1) Smaller initial bundle size — faster first paint (2) Reduced memory usage — unused code isn't loaded (3) Better user experience on slow networks (4) Improved Core Web Vitals scores. Downside: slight delay when the lazy-loaded chunk is first requested. Solution: use preloading strategies to load chunks in the background.

Lighthouse is a browser DevTool that audits web pages for Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, SEO, and PWA readiness. It gives scores (0-100) and specific recommendations. Key metrics: FCP (First Contentful Paint), LCP (Largest Contentful Paint), CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift), TBT (Total Blocking Time). Use it to: identify slow-loading resources, find accessibility issues, detect SEO problems, and measure real-world performance. Run it via Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse tab → Generate Report.

Sharding is a database scaling technique that distributes data across multiple servers (shards). Each shard holds a portion of the data. For example, users A-M on Shard 1, N-Z on Shard 2. Benefits: horizontal scaling, better performance for large datasets, geographic distribution. In MongoDB, you choose a shard key (e.g., user_id) that determines which shard holds each document. Types: Range-based sharding (ranges of values), Hash-based sharding (hash of the shard key for even distribution).

Authentication verifies WHO you are. Authorization verifies WHAT you can access. Flow: (1) User sends credentials (email/password) to login API (2) Server validates credentials against the database (3) Server generates a JWT token containing user info (4) Token is sent back to client and stored (localStorage/cookie) (5) Client sends token in Authorization header with every request (6) Server validates token on each request (middleware) (7) If valid, grant access; if expired/invalid, return 401. Common methods: Session-based, JWT, OAuth 2.0, SSO.

Pseudo-elements style specific parts of an element. Pseudo-classes style an element based on its state.

Pseudo-elements (::) — create virtual elements:
::before — inserts content before the element
::after — inserts content after the element
::first-line — styles the first line of text
::placeholder — styles input placeholder text

Pseudo-classes (:) — based on state:
:hover — mouse is over the element
:focus — element is focused
:nth-child(n) — targets nth child
:first-child / :last-child
:disabled — for disabled inputs

Key difference: :: creates something new, : selects existing state.

Throttle executes a function at most once every X milliseconds — it fires at a regular interval during continuous events. Debounce waits until X milliseconds have passed since the LAST call.

Throttle: Good for scroll events, window resize — limits how often a function runs.
Debounce: Good for search input, form validation — waits for the user to stop.

Example: User types 'hello' (5 keystrokes in 1 second)
- Throttle (300ms): fires at 0ms, 300ms, 600ms = 3 calls
- Debounce (300ms): fires once at 1300ms (300ms after last keystroke) = 1 call

In RxJS: throttleTime(300) and debounceTime(300).

AOT (Ahead-of-Time) compiles templates during the build process BEFORE the browser downloads the app. JIT (Just-in-Time) compiles templates in the browser at runtime.

AOT advantages: Faster rendering (templates pre-compiled), smaller bundle (compiler not shipped), detect template errors at build time, better security (no eval).

JIT advantages: Faster development builds, no need to rebuild for template changes.

Angular uses AOT by default for production (ng build --prod) and JIT for development (ng serve). AOT is always preferred for production deployments.

AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs your code in response to events without provisioning or managing servers. You upload your code, and Lambda handles scaling, patching, and infrastructure. Key features: (1) Pay only for compute time used (per ms) (2) Auto-scales from 0 to thousands of instances (3) Triggered by events: API Gateway, S3 uploads, DynamoDB changes, scheduled cron (4) Supports Node.js, Python, Java, Go, .NET (5) Max execution time: 15 minutes. Use cases: API backends, file processing, scheduled tasks, webhooks.

Worker Threads in Node.js run JavaScript in parallel threads — ideal for CPU-intensive tasks. Alternatives for child processes:

1. worker_threads: True parallel threads, share memory via SharedArrayBuffer
2. child_process.fork(): Spawns a new Node.js process with IPC communication
3. child_process.exec(): Runs a shell command, returns stdout/stderr
4. child_process.spawn(): Streams data from a command (good for large outputs)
5. cluster module: Forks multiple instances of the app for load balancing

Use worker_threads for CPU tasks (image processing, compression). Use child_process for running external commands or separate Node scripts. Use cluster for scaling HTTP servers across CPU cores.

Yes! HTML5 <video> and <audio> tags provide native media playback.

<video width='640' controls>
  <source src='movie.mp4' type='video/mp4'>
  <source src='movie.webm' type='video/webm'>
  Your browser does not support video.
</video>

<audio controls>
  <source src='audio.mp3' type='audio/mpeg'>
</audio>

Key attributes: controls (show player UI), autoplay, loop, muted, poster (thumbnail image), preload (none/metadata/auto).

JavaScript API: video.play(), video.pause(), video.currentTime, video.duration, video.volume. Events: onplay, onpause, onended, ontimeupdate.

OWASP (Open Web Application Security Project — likely what the interviewer meant by 'WASP') provides the Top 10 web application security risks: (1) Injection (SQL, NoSQL, XSS) (2) Broken Authentication (3) Sensitive Data Exposure (4) XML External Entities (5) Broken Access Control (6) Security Misconfiguration (7) Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) (8) Insecure Deserialization (9) Using Components with Known Vulnerabilities (10) Insufficient Logging. Every web developer should know these and implement defenses: input validation, parameterized queries, HTTPS, proper auth, CSP headers, etc.

Paint Profiler (in Chrome DevTools Performance tab) shows how the browser paints pixels on screen. It records paint operations (draw rectangles, draw text, draw images) and shows: (1) Which elements triggered paint (2) Time spent painting each layer (3) Paint complexity per frame. To use: DevTools → Performance → Record → interact with page → Stop → click a paint event in the flame chart. Useful for: finding paint bottlenecks, identifying elements causing excessive repaints, optimizing CSS animations (use transform/opacity which skip paint). Avoid: box-shadow changes, border-radius animations, background-color transitions on large elements.

Performance Recording in Chrome DevTools captures a timeline of everything happening in the browser. Press Record, interact with your page, then Stop. It shows: (1) Flame chart — JavaScript execution, function calls with time (2) FPS meter — frames per second (target: 60fps) (3) CPU usage timeline (4) Network requests timing (5) Layout/Paint/Composite phases (6) Long tasks (>50ms) highlighted in red. Key metrics: Scripting time, Rendering time, Painting time, Idle time. Use it to find: slow functions, layout thrashing, memory leaks, janky animations. Most important optimization target: reduce main thread blocking.

BookMyShow seat blocking — Real-time seat reservation pattern:

1. Optimistic Locking: When user selects seat → temporarily lock it in DB with a TTL (e.g., 10 minutes). Set status to 'HELD' with user_id and expires_at timestamp.

2. WebSocket/SSE: Broadcast seat status changes to all connected users in real-time. When a seat is held/booked, other users see it as unavailable instantly.

3. Database level:
UPDATE seats SET status='HELD', held_by=userId, held_until=NOW()+10min
WHERE seat_id=X AND status='AVAILABLE'

If affected rows = 0, seat was already taken → show error.

4. Payment timeout: If payment not completed within TTL, a cron job releases the seat back to 'AVAILABLE'.

5. Use Redis for fast seat status checks + pub/sub for real-time updates.

Higher Order Functions (HOF) are functions that take a function as an argument or return a function.

Built-in HOFs:
map: [1,2,3].map(x => x * 2) // [2, 4, 6]
filter: [1,2,3,4].filter(x => x > 2) // [3, 4]
reduce: [1,2,3].reduce((sum, x) => sum + x, 0) // 6
forEach: arr.forEach(item => console.log(item))
sort: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)

Custom HOF:
function multiplier(factor) {
  return (number) => number * factor; // returns a function
}
const double = multiplier(2);
double(5); // 10
double(10); // 20

HOFs enable composition, reusability, and functional programming patterns.

Agile is an iterative software development methodology focused on delivering small, incremental improvements through collaboration and feedback. Key concepts:

Sprints: 2-4 week development cycles
Scrum ceremonies: Sprint Planning, Daily Standup (15 min), Sprint Review, Retrospective
Roles: Product Owner (what to build), Scrum Master (process), Dev Team (how to build)
Artifacts: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment

Agile vs Waterfall: Agile is iterative, flexible, delivers frequently. Waterfall is sequential, rigid, delivers at the end.

Tools: Jira, Azure DevOps, Trello. Story points estimate effort. Velocity tracks team speed per sprint.

Recent Angular improvements: Angular 16: Signals for reactive state management, required inputs, DestroyRef for cleanup. Angular 17: New control flow syntax (@if, @for, @switch replacing *ngIf, *ngFor), deferrable views (@defer for lazy loading sections), built-in SSR improvements, new app builder (esbuild replacing webpack — 87% faster builds), standalone components as default. Angular 18: Zoneless change detection (experimental), improved hydration, Material 3 components. Angular 19: Incremental hydration, resource API, linkedSignal. Overall trend: simpler APIs, better performance, smaller bundles, moving away from NgModules toward standalone.

Accessibility (a11y) in Angular ensures your app is usable by people with disabilities. Key practices: (1) Semantic HTML — use <button>, <nav>, <main> instead of generic <div> (2) ARIA attributes — role, aria-label, aria-describedby, aria-live (3) Keyboard navigation — all interactions must work via Tab, Enter, Escape (4) Focus management — manage focus when routes change or modals open (5) Angular CDK a11y module — FocusTrap, LiveAnnouncer, FocusMonitor (6) Color contrast — WCAG 2.1 minimum 4.5:1 ratio (7) Alt text on images (8) Form labels — every input needs an associated <label>. Test with: Lighthouse, axe DevTools, screen readers (NVDA, VoiceOver).

State management options in Angular UI:

1. Component state: Simple @Input/@Output for parent-child.
2. Services with BehaviorSubject: For shared state across components.
   private state$ = new BehaviorSubject<AppState>(initialState);
3. NgRx: Full Redux pattern — Store, Actions, Reducers, Effects, Selectors. Best for complex apps.
4. Signals (Angular 16+): Fine-grained reactivity.
   count = signal(0);
   increment() { this.count.update(v => v + 1); }
5. NGXS: Simpler alternative to NgRx.
6. Akita: Entity-based state management.

Choose based on complexity: Simple app → Services + BehaviorSubject. Medium → Signals. Complex → NgRx/NGXS.

Pure pipes (default) only execute when the input value REFERENCE changes. Impure pipes execute on every change detection cycle.

Pure pipe: @Pipe({ name: 'myPipe', pure: true }) — Angular caches the result. If you pass the same input, it returns the cached output without re-executing. Great for performance.

Impure pipe: @Pipe({ name: 'myPipe', pure: false }) — Runs on every change detection. Needed when the pipe depends on external state or when input is mutated (not replaced).

Example problem: A pure pipe filtering an array won't update when you push() to the array (same reference). Solutions: (1) Use impure pipe (2) Replace array: this.items = [...this.items, newItem] (3) Use async pipe with Observable.

Rule: Use pure pipes whenever possible for performance.

Angular 17 architecture changes: (1) Standalone-first — no AppModule by default, components declare their own imports (2) New app builder — uses esbuild + Vite instead of webpack (87% faster builds) (3) New control flow — @if, @for, @switch replace structural directives (4) Deferrable views — @defer loads sections lazily with @loading, @placeholder, @error states (5) Signals integration — reactive primitives for state (6) SSR improvements — hydration for server-rendered content (7) New project structure — app.config.ts replaces AppModule, app.routes.ts for routing. The goal: simpler, faster, more intuitive development experience.

Angular 16 changes: Signals (reactive primitives), required inputs (@Input({ required: true })), DestroyRef, takeUntilDestroyed(). Angular 17 changes: New control flow (@if, @for, @switch), @defer for lazy sections, esbuild by default (faster builds), standalone components as default, new SSR with hydration. Common across both: Move away from NgModules, better performance, simpler APIs, improved developer experience. The trend is making Angular simpler and more like modern frameworks while keeping its enterprise strengths.

SSR (Server-Side Rendering): HTML is generated on the server and sent fully rendered to the browser. Benefits: Better SEO (crawlers see full HTML), faster First Contentful Paint, works without JavaScript. Used in Angular Universal.

CSR (Client-Side Rendering): Browser downloads a minimal HTML shell + JavaScript bundle, then JS builds the DOM. Benefits: Rich interactivity, smoother navigation after initial load, less server load.

SSR flow: Request → Server renders HTML → Send to browser → Hydration (attach JS events)
CSR flow: Request → Empty HTML + JS bundle → Browser executes JS → Renders DOM

When to use SSR: Content-heavy sites, SEO-critical pages, blogs. When to use CSR: Dashboards, admin panels, SPAs behind login. Angular 17+ has improved SSR with hydration support built-in.

Use Observable over Promise when you need: (1) Multiple values over time — Promises resolve once, Observables emit multiple times (2) Cancellation — call unsubscribe() to cancel, Promises can't be cancelled (3) Operators — map, filter, retry, debounce, switchMap etc. (4) Lazy execution — Observables don't execute until subscribed (5) Composition — combine multiple streams easily.

Real examples where Promise fails:
- WebSocket messages (continuous stream)
- Search autocomplete (cancel previous, debounce)
- Real-time dashboard updates
- Retry failed HTTP requests
- Combining multiple event sources

Angular's HttpClient returns Observables by default. For simple one-off async operations, Promises are fine. For anything reactive or stream-based, Observables win.

ReplaySubject: Replays a specified number of previous values to new subscribers.
const rs = new ReplaySubject(2); // Buffer last 2 values
rs.next(1); rs.next(2); rs.next(3);
rs.subscribe(v => console.log(v)); // Prints 2, 3 (last 2)

BehaviorSubject: Always has a current value. New subscribers get the LATEST value immediately.
const bs = new BehaviorSubject(0); // Requires initial value
bs.next(1); bs.next(2);
bs.subscribe(v => console.log(v)); // Prints 2 (current value)
bs.getValue(); // 2 — synchronous access

Key differences:
- BehaviorSubject requires initial value, ReplaySubject doesn't
- BehaviorSubject replays 1 value, ReplaySubject replays N values
- BehaviorSubject has getValue(), ReplaySubject doesn't

Use BehaviorSubject for current state (auth, settings). Use ReplaySubject for event history (chat messages, logs).

NgRx is a state management library for Angular based on the Redux pattern. Architecture:

Store: Single source of truth — holds the application state.
Actions: Events that describe something that happened (e.g., '[User] Load Users').
Reducers: Pure functions that take current state + action and return new state.
Effects: Handle side effects (API calls, navigation) — listen for actions, perform async work, dispatch new actions.
Selectors: Functions to extract specific pieces of state.

Flow: Component dispatches Action → Reducer updates Store → Selector reads Store → Component displays data.
For side effects: Action → Effect → API call → Effect dispatches success/failure Action → Reducer updates Store.

Install: ng add @ngrx/store @ngrx/effects @ngrx/store-devtools

Use NgRx when: Multiple components share complex state, many user interactions, heavy API coordination.

Node.js event loop architecture flow:

1. Timers phase: Execute setTimeout/setInterval callbacks
2. Pending callbacks: Execute I/O callbacks deferred from previous cycle
3. Idle/Prepare: Internal use only
4. Poll phase: Retrieve new I/O events, execute I/O callbacks. Node blocks here when there's nothing else to do
5. Check phase: Execute setImmediate() callbacks
6. Close callbacks: Execute close event callbacks (socket.on('close'))

Between each phase: Process all microtasks (Promise callbacks, process.nextTick)

Priority: process.nextTick > Promise.then > setTimeout/setImmediate > I/O callbacks

Node.js is single-threaded for JavaScript execution but uses libuv's thread pool (default 4 threads) for file I/O, DNS lookups, and crypto operations.

Microservices communicate via:

1. HTTP/REST: Simple request-response. Service A calls Service B's API.
axios.get('http://user-service:3001/api/users/123')

2. Message Queues (async): RabbitMQ, AWS SQS, Kafka. Service A publishes message, Service B consumes.
Best for: decoupled, reliable, handles failures.

3. gRPC: High-performance binary protocol. Faster than REST, supports streaming.

4. Event-driven: Services publish events to a broker (Kafka, Redis Pub/Sub). Other services subscribe.

5. API Gateway: Single entry point routes requests to correct microservice.

Sync vs Async:
- Sync (REST/gRPC): Immediate response needed. Simpler but creates coupling.
- Async (Message Queue/Events): Fire and forget. Better resilience, loose coupling.

Service discovery: Kubernetes DNS, Consul, or environment variables for finding service URLs.

Improve Node.js app performance:

1. Caching: Redis for frequently accessed data
2. Database optimization: Indexes, query optimization, connection pooling
3. Clustering: Use cluster module to utilize all CPU cores
4. Load balancing: Nginx or PM2 in cluster mode
5. Compression: gzip/brotli middleware for responses
6. Streaming: Stream large files instead of loading into memory
7. Async patterns: Avoid blocking the event loop
8. Connection pooling: Reuse DB connections
9. Rate limiting: Prevent abuse with express-rate-limit
10. Monitoring: Use clinic.js, node --prof for profiling
11. Memory management: Fix leaks, optimize garbage collection
12. CDN: Serve static assets from CDN
13. HTTP/2: Multiplexing, server push
14. Worker threads: Offload CPU-heavy tasks
15. Code-level: Avoid synchronous methods, use efficient algorithms

Choose Node.js when: (1) Real-time applications — chat, gaming, live dashboards (WebSocket support) (2) API servers — REST/GraphQL APIs with high I/O (3) Microservices — lightweight, fast startup (4) Streaming — video/audio streaming, file processing (5) Single language — JavaScript on both frontend and backend (6) High concurrency — thousands of simultaneous connections (non-blocking I/O).

Don't choose Node.js when: (1) CPU-intensive computation — video encoding, ML training, heavy math (2) Relational data-heavy apps — better with Java/Python + SQL (3) Enterprise with strict typing needs — consider Java/.NET (though TypeScript helps).

Why Node.js? V8 engine is fast, npm has 2M+ packages, single-threaded event loop handles I/O efficiently, great for JSON-based APIs, huge community.

Security best practices for Node.js apps:

1. Use helmet: Sets security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options, HSTS)
2. Input validation: Validate/sanitize all inputs (express-validator, joi)
3. SQL/NoSQL injection prevention: Use parameterized queries, Mongoose schemas
4. Authentication: JWT or session-based with bcrypt for passwords
5. HTTPS: Always use TLS in production
6. Rate limiting: express-rate-limit to prevent brute force
7. CORS: Configure properly — never allow all origins in production
8. Dependencies: npm audit regularly, use Snyk
9. Environment variables: Never hardcode secrets, use dotenv
10. Error handling: Don't expose stack traces to clients
11. Cookie security: httpOnly, secure, sameSite flags
12. CSRF protection: Use tokens for form submissions
13. File uploads: Validate type/size, use multer with limits
14. Logging: Winston/Morgan for audit trails
15. Keep Node.js updated: Security patches

npm: Node Package Manager — installs and manages packages.
npx: Node Package Execute — runs packages without installing globally.

npm install create-react-app → Installs globally, takes disk space
npx create-react-app my-app → Downloads temporarily, runs, then removes

Key differences:
npm install -g typescript → Installs globally, may get outdated
npx tsc --init → Always uses the latest version

npm: Use for project dependencies (npm install express)
npx: Use for one-time commands (npx create-next-app, npx eslint --init)

npx first checks if the package exists locally (node_modules/.bin), then globally, then downloads temporarily. This ensures you always run the latest version without polluting global installs.

Clear memory and handle memory leaks in Node.js:

1. Identify leaks: Use --inspect flag + Chrome DevTools Memory tab, or clinic.js.

2. Common causes and fixes:
- Global variables: Avoid storing data in global scope. Use let/const.
- Event listeners not removed: Always removeListener or use { once: true }.
- Closures holding references: Be careful with callbacks capturing large objects.
- Unclosed connections: Close DB connections, streams, timers.
- Caching without limits: Use LRU cache with max size.

3. Force garbage collection (debugging only):
node --expose-gc app.js
global.gc();

4. Monitor memory:
const used = process.memoryUsage();
console.log(`Heap: ${Math.round(used.heapUsed / 1024 / 1024)}MB`);

5. Set max memory: node --max-old-space-size=4096 app.js

6. Use WeakMap/WeakRef for objects that should be garbage collected when no longer referenced.

SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) is a structured process for building software. Phases:

1. Planning: Define scope, feasibility, timeline, budget
2. Requirements Analysis: Gather and document what the software should do (BRD, SRS)
3. Design: Architecture, database design, UI mockups (HLD, LLD)
4. Development: Write code, implement features
5. Testing: Unit testing, integration testing, UAT
6. Deployment: Release to production (CI/CD pipelines)
7. Maintenance: Bug fixes, updates, monitoring

SDLC Models:
- Waterfall: Sequential, no going back. Good for fixed requirements.
- Agile: Iterative sprints, flexible. Most popular today.
- V-Model: Testing at each stage.
- Spiral: Risk-driven, prototyping.
- DevOps: Continuous integration and delivery.

Most companies today use Agile with 2-week sprints.

CI/CD pipeline for deploying Node.js changes:

CI (Continuous Integration): Automatically build and test on every push.
CD (Continuous Deployment): Automatically deploy after tests pass.

Typical pipeline (GitHub Actions):
1. Developer pushes code → triggers pipeline
2. Install dependencies (npm ci)
3. Lint code (eslint)
4. Run unit tests (jest)
5. Run integration tests

Tools: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, AWS CodePipeline.
Deployment targets: AWS (ECS, Lambda, EC2), GCP, Azure, Heroku, Render, Railway.
Containerization: Docker + Kubernetes for orchestration.

Key practices: Feature branches, pull request reviews, automated tests as gate, blue-green deployments, rollback strategy.

Drawbacks of MongoDB:

1. No ACID transactions across collections (improved in v4.0+ but still slower than SQL)
2. No joins natively — $lookup is slower than SQL JOINs
3. Data duplication — denormalization leads to larger storage and update complexity
4. No schema enforcement by default — can lead to inconsistent data (use Mongoose schemas)
5. Memory hungry — indexes must fit in RAM for good performance
6. Not ideal for highly relational data — many-to-many relationships are awkward
7. Aggregation pipeline has a learning curve
8. Limited to 16MB per document
9. No stored procedures (like SQL)
10. Write conflicts in replica sets during network partitions

When NOT to use MongoDB: Banking/financial systems needing strict ACID, highly relational data, complex reporting with many JOINs.

When to use: Flexible schemas, rapid prototyping, real-time analytics, content management, IoT data.

Optimize MongoDB queries:

1. Indexes: Create indexes for frequently queried fields. Use explain() to verify.
db.users.find({ email: 'test@test.com' }).explain('executionStats');

2. Compound indexes: Follow the ESR rule (Equality → Sort → Range).

3. Projection: Only return fields you need.
db.users.find({}, { name: 1, email: 1 }); // Don't fetch entire document

4. Limit and skip: Paginate results.
db.posts.find().sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20).skip(40);

5. Lean queries (Mongoose): Skip hydration for read-only data.
User.find({}).lean(); // Returns plain objects, 5x faster

6. Avoid $regex without prefix: /^term/ uses index, /term/ does not.

7. Use aggregation $match early in pipeline to filter before processing.

8. Connection pooling: Reuse connections.

9. Covered queries: When index contains all queried fields — no document fetch needed.

10. Monitor with MongoDB Atlas Performance Advisor or Profiler.

Sharding distributes data across multiple servers. A Cluster is the complete MongoDB deployment.

Sharding components:
1. Shard servers: Hold portions of the data
2. Config servers: Store metadata about which shard has which data
3. mongos (router): Routes queries to the correct shard

Shard key: The field used to distribute data (e.g., userId, region).

Types:
- Range sharding: Consecutive values on same shard. Good for range queries.
- Hashed sharding: Hash of shard key. Even distribution but no range queries.

When to shard: (1) Single server can't handle data size (2) Read/write throughput exceeds single server capacity (3) Need geographic distribution.

Caution: Sharding adds complexity. Don't shard until you need it. Try replica sets + read preferences first. Once sharded, changing the shard key is very difficult.

Index field order matters significantly in MongoDB compound indexes.

Index: { category: 1, price: 1, rating: -1 }

This query uses the full index:
db.products.find({ category: 'electronics', price: { $lt: 500 } }).sort({ rating: -1 });

This uses partial index (first 2 fields):
db.products.find({ category: 'electronics', price: { $lt: 500 } });

This uses only prefix (first field):
db.products.find({ category: 'electronics' });

This CANNOT use the index (missing prefix):
db.products.find({ price: { $lt: 500 } }); // Full collection scan!

The ESR Rule for optimal ordering:
E (Equality) → fields with exact match (=)
S (Sort) → fields used in sort()
R (Range) → fields with range operators ($gt, $lt, $in)

Example: { status: 1, createdAt: -1, amount: 1 } for queries that filter by status, sort by date, and range filter by amount. Always put equality fields first — they narrow down results the most.

Upgrading Angular, Node.js, and MongoDB versions:

Angular upgrade:
1. Check compatibility: Visit update.angular.io for step-by-step guide
2. Update CLI: ng update @angular/cli @angular/core
3. Update dependencies: ng update (shows available updates)
4. Fix breaking changes: Follow migration guide
5. Run tests: ng test && ng build

Node.js upgrade:
1. Use nvm: nvm install 20 && nvm use 20
2. Update package.json engines field
3. Run npm install to rebuild native modules
4. Test thoroughly — check for deprecated APIs

MongoDB upgrade:
1. Check compatibility matrix between driver and server
2. Upgrade driver first: npm install mongoose@latest
3. Upgrade server: Follow MongoDB upgrade path (can't skip major versions)
4. Update connection string if needed
5. Test queries and indexes

A JWT token has 3 parts separated by dots: xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz

1. Header (xxxxx): Contains token type and signing algorithm.
{ "alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT" }
Base64Url encoded.

2. Payload (yyyyy): Contains claims — data about the user.
{ "sub": "1234567890", "name": "Siva", "role": "admin", "iat": 1516239022, "exp": 1516242622 }
Standard claims: iss (issuer), exp (expiry), sub (subject), iat (issued at).
Base64Url encoded. NOT encrypted — anyone can decode it!

3. Signature (zzzzz): Verifies the token wasn't tampered with.
HMACSHA256(base64UrlEncode(header) + '.' + base64UrlEncode(payload), secret)

Full token: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJuYW1lIjoiU2l2YSJ9.signature

IMPORTANT: JWT payload is NOT encrypted — never put passwords or sensitive data in it. The signature only ensures integrity, not secrecy.

JWT vs other authentication methods:

JWT (JSON Web Token):
- Stateless — server doesn't store sessions
- Token contains user data (self-contained)
- Scales easily across multiple servers
- Best for: APIs, microservices, mobile apps

Session-based:
- Stateful — server stores session in memory/DB
- Session ID sent via cookie
- Server must look up session on each request
- Best for: Traditional web apps, single-server setups

OAuth 2.0:
- Delegated authorization — third-party login
- 'Login with Google/GitHub'
- Complex flow with authorization codes
- Best for: Third-party integrations

SSO (Single Sign-On):
- One login for multiple applications
- Uses SAML or OpenID Connect
- Best for: Enterprise with many internal apps

JWT is most popular for modern APIs because it's stateless and works great with microservices. Session-based is simpler for monolithic web apps.

rem, em, and px are CSS units for sizing:

px (pixels): Absolute unit. 16px is always 16px regardless of context.
font-size: 16px; // Always 16 pixels

em: Relative to the PARENT element's font size.
parent { font-size: 16px; }
child { font-size: 1.5em; } // 24px (16 × 1.5)
grandchild { font-size: 1.5em; } // 36px (24 × 1.5) — compounds!

rem (root em): Relative to the ROOT element's (html) font size. Consistent and predictable.
html { font-size: 16px; }
.heading { font-size: 2rem; } // Always 32px
.text { font-size: 1rem; } // Always 16px

Best practices:
- Use rem for font-size (consistent, accessible — users can change root font)
- Use em for padding/margin relative to text size
- Use px for borders, shadows, and precise measurements
- Common pattern: html { font-size: 62.5%; } makes 1rem = 10px for easy math

Webpack is a module bundler for JavaScript applications. It takes modules with dependencies and generates static assets.

What it does: Takes your source files (JS, CSS, images, HTML) → processes them through loaders and plugins → outputs optimized bundles for the browser.

Core concepts:
1. Entry: Starting point (e.g., src/index.js)
2. Output: Where bundled files go (e.g., dist/bundle.js)
3. Loaders: Transform files (babel-loader for JS, css-loader for CSS, ts-loader for TypeScript)
4. Plugins: Perform broader tasks (HtmlWebpackPlugin, MiniCssExtractPlugin, DefinePlugin)
5. Mode: development (readable) or production (minified)

Why use it:
- Bundle many files into few (reduces HTTP requests)
- Tree shaking (remove unused code)
- Code splitting (lazy loading)
- Asset optimization (minify, compress)
- Dev server with hot reload

Alternatives: Vite (faster, uses esbuild), esbuild, Rollup, Parcel. Angular 17+ switched from Webpack to esbuild for 87% faster builds.

npm install vs npm ci:

npm install:
- Reads package.json
- Installs dependencies and updates package-lock.json
- Can install different versions (within semver range)
- If node_modules exists, updates it incrementally
- Slower but flexible
- Use for: Development, adding new packages

npm ci (clean install):
- Reads package-lock.json (ignores package.json ranges)
- Deletes node_modules completely, then installs fresh
- Installs EXACT versions from lock file
- Fails if package-lock.json is out of sync with package.json
- Faster and deterministic
- Use for: CI/CD pipelines, production builds, team collaboration

// Development workflow
npm install lodash // Add package, update lock file
npm install // Install all, may update versions

// CI/CD pipeline
npm ci // Exact reproducible install, always clean
npm run test
npm run build

Rule: Use npm ci in CI/CD and Docker builds. Use npm install during development.
